hollandsk.explanation: "Hollandsk" means "Dutch". It comes from "Holland" (the Netherlands). To say what language you speak, put it after "taler" (speak): "Jeg taler hollandsk" (I speak Dutch).

honning.explanation: "Honning" means "honey". To say what is on your bread, use "på" (on): "Jeg har honning på brødet" (I have honey on my bread).

hos.explanation: "Hos" means "at". When you say you are at a person's home or practice, put the person after it: "hos min ven" (at my friend's place) and "hos lægen" (at the doctor's). To say you are at a building, use "på" (at) instead: "Jeg er på biblioteket" (I am at the library).

hovedsagelig.explanation: "Hovedsagelig" means "mainly". The start "hoved" means "main" in other words, such as "hovedgade" (main street).

hovedsageligt.explanation: "Hovedsageligt" means "mainly". The start "hoved" means "main" in other words, such as "hovedgade" (main street).

hud.explanation: "Hud" means "skin". It takes "en": "en hud". To say your skin is dry, use "tør" (dry): "Jeg har tør hud" (I have dry skin).

humor.explanation: "Humor" means "humor". To say someone has a sense of humor, use "sans" (sense) with "for" (for): "Hun har sans for humor" (She has a sense of humor).

humoristisk.explanation: "Humoristisk" means "humorous". It comes from "humor" (humor). To say something was fun, use "sjov" (fun) instead: "Det var sjovt!" (That was fun!)

hun.explanation: "Hun" means "she". When she does the action, use "hun": "Hun hjælper mig" (She helps me). When she receives the action, use "hende" (her): "Jeg hjælper hende" (I help her).

hundemad.explanation: "Hundemad" means "dog food". It is built from "hund" (dog) and "mad" (food). The word "mad" also ends "morgenmad" (breakfast) and "aftensmad" (dinner).

hundrede.explanation: "Hundrede" means "hundred". To say 200 or 300, put the number first and keep "hundrede" the same: "to hundrede" (200) and "tre hundrede" (300). To say 100, just say "hundrede"; no "en" (one) is needed.

hundrededel.explanation: "Hundrededel" means "a hundredth". It is built from "hundrede" (hundred) and "del" (part). To say a tenth, use the same pattern: "en tiendedel" (a tenth).

hurra.explanation: "Hurra" means "hooray". To cheer together, say "hip hip hurra" (hip hip hooray).

hurtig.explanation: "Hurtig" means "fast". To say how someone does an action, use "hurtigt" (fast) instead: "Han løber hurtigt" (He runs fast).

husarbejde.explanation: "Husarbejde" means "housework". It is built from "hus" (house) and "arbejde" (work). To say you have a new job, use "arbejde" alone: "Jeg har et nyt arbejde" (I have a new job).

husholdningsfilm.explanation: "Husholdningsfilm" means "plastic wrap". It is built from "husholdning" (household) and "film". Here "film" means a thin sheet, not a movie.

husleje.explanation: "Husleje" means "rent". It is built from "hus" (house) and "leje" (hire). To say you rent a car, use the verb "at leje" (to rent): "Jeg vil gerne leje en bil" (I would like to rent a car).

hvabehar.explanation: "Hvabehar" means "pardon". It comes from "hvad behager", which literally means "what pleases". To show surprise, say it sharply: "Hvabehar! Er det sandt?" (What! Is it true?)

hvad.explanation: "Hvad" means "what". To ask about a thing, use "hvad": "Hvad er det?" (What is that?). To ask about a person, use "hvem" (who) instead: "Hvem er det?" (Who is that?). When you did not hear something, "Hvad?" (What?) is blunt. "Undskyld?" (Excuse me?) is more polite.

hvad betyder det?.explanation: "Hvad betyder det?" means "What does that mean?". It is built from "hvad" (what), "betyder" (means) and "det" (that).

hvad er klokken?.explanation: "Hvad er klokken?" means "What time is it?". Literally, it asks "what is the clock", because "klokken" means "the clock".

hvad hedder det på dansk?.explanation: "Hvad hedder det på dansk?" means "What is that called in Danish?". The verb "hedder" (is called) is also used for names. To say your own name, say: "Jeg hedder Anna" (My name is Anna).

hvad hedder du?.explanation: "Hvad hedder du?" means "What's your name?". Literally, it asks what you are called. The verb in it is "hedder" (are called).

hvad koster det?.explanation: "Hvad koster det?" means "How much does it cost?". To ask about something that takes "et", such as "et hus" (a house), use "det" (it): "Hvad koster det?" To ask about something that takes "en", such as "en bog" (a book), use "den" (it): "Hvad koster den?" (How much does it cost?) To ask about several things, use "de" (they): "Hvad koster de?" (How much do they cost?)

hvad laver du?.explanation: "Hvad laver du?" means "What are you doing?". To ask about someone's work, say "Hvad arbejder du med?" (What do you work with?). To ask several people, use "I" (you all): "Hvad laver I?" (What are you all doing?)

related.en: what are you going to do?

hvad med dig?.explanation: "Hvad med dig?" means "What about you?". Literally, it is "what with you". To ask about a person by name, put the name in place of "dig" (you): "Hvad med Anna?" (What about Anna?)

hvad som helst.explanation: "Hvad som helst" means "anything". To say any person, use "hvem som helst" (anyone) instead: "Hvem som helst kan komme" (Anyone can come).

hvad så?.explanation: "Hvad så?" means "What's up?". Literally, it is "what then", because "så" means "then" here. The same "så" means "so" in other places: "Jeg er så glad" (I am so happy).

hvede.explanation: "Hvede" means "wheat". It also starts other words, such as "hvedebrød" (wheat bread) and "hvedemel" (wheat flour).

hvedemel.explanation: "Hvedemel" means "wheat flour". It is built from "hvede" (wheat) and "mel" (flour). Another word that starts with "hvede" is "hvedebrød" (wheat bread).

hvem.explanation: "Hvem" means "who". English has two forms, "who" and "whom", but Danish uses "hvem" for both. When it asks who does the action, say: "Hvem taler?" (Who is speaking?) When it asks who is spoken to, say: "Hvem taler du med?" (To whom are you speaking?) To ask about a thing, use "hvad" (what) instead: "Hvad spiser du?" (What are you eating?)

hvem som helst.explanation: "Hvem som helst" means "anyone". To say anything, use "hvad som helst" (anything) instead: "Jeg spiser hvad som helst" (I eat anything).

hver.explanation: "Hver" means "every". Put it before a word that takes "en", such as "en dag" (a day): "hver dag" (every day). For a word that takes "et", use "hvert" instead: "hvert år" (every year).

hver dag.explanation: "Hver dag" means "every day". It is built from "hver" (every) and "dag" (day). To say every second day, put "anden" (other) between them: "hver anden dag" (every other day).

hverken.explanation: "Hverken" means "neither". It is used with "eller" (nor) as a pair: "hverken A eller B" (neither A nor B). To say you have neither of two things, say: "Jeg har hverken tid eller penge" (I have neither time nor money).

hverken…eller.explanation: "Hverken…eller" means "neither…nor". To say you have neither of two things, put "hverken" before the first and "eller" before the second: "Jeg har hverken tid eller penge" (I have neither time nor money). Do not add "ikke" (not), because the sentence already says no.

hvert.explanation: "Hvert" means "every". Put it before a word that takes "et", such as "et år" (a year): "hvert år" (every year). For a word that takes "en", use "hver" instead: "hver dag" (every day).

hvid.explanation: "Hvid" means "white". It also starts "hvidløg" (garlic), which is literally white onion.

hvidløg.explanation: "Hvidløg" means "garlic". It is built from "hvid" (white) and "løg" (onion). To count garlic, use "et fed" (a clove): "to fed hvidløg" (two cloves of garlic).

hvilke.explanation: "Hvilke" means "which". Put it before a word that names more than one thing: "hvilke skoler" (which schools). To ask about one thing that takes "en", use "hvilken": "hvilken bil" (which car). For one thing that takes "et", use "hvilket": "hvilket hus" (which house).

hvilken.explanation: "Hvilken" means "which". Put it before a word that takes "en", such as "en bil" (a car): "Hvilken bil vil du have?" (Which car do you want?) For a word that takes "et", use "hvilket" instead: "Hvilket hus?" (Which house?) When no word follows, use "hvad" (what): "Hvad vil du have?" (What do you want?)

hvilket.explanation: "Hvilket" means "which". Put it before a word that takes "et", such as "et land" (a country): "Hvilket land kommer du fra?" (Which country are you from?) For a word that takes "en", use "hvilken" instead: "Hvilken bil?" (Which car?)

hvis.explanation: "Hvis" means "if". To say a condition, put "hvis" before it: "Hvis jeg har tid, kommer jeg" (If I have time, I will come). Do not mix it up with "om" (whether): "Jeg ved ikke, om han kommer" (I do not know whether he is coming).

hvis jeg var dig.explanation: "Hvis jeg var dig" means "if I were you". To give advice, start with it and then say what you would do: "Hvis jeg var dig, ville jeg ringe til ham" (If I were you, I would call him). The verb "var" (was) is used here where English says "were".

hvor.explanation: "Hvor" means "where". To ask "how" about a quality or an amount, put "hvor" before the word: "hvor gammel" (how old), "hvor mange" (how many).

hvor er toilettet?.explanation: "Hvor er toilettet?" means "Where is the restroom?". It is built from "hvor" (where), "er" (is) and "toilettet" (the toilet), where the ending "-et" means "the".

hvor gammel er du?.explanation: "Hvor gammel er du?" means "How old are you?". It is built from "hvor" (how), "gammel" (old), "er" (are) and "du" (you). To say your age, you can leave out "gammel": "Jeg er tyve år" (I am twenty years old).

hvor kommer du fra?.explanation: "Hvor kommer du fra?" means "Where are you from?". Literally, it asks where you come from. To answer, say: "Jeg kommer fra England" (I come from England). The word "fra" (from) stays at the end of the question, as in English.

hvor meget koster det?.explanation: "Hvor meget koster det?" means "How much does it cost?". Word by word, it is "how much costs it". To ask about weight, use the same start with another verb: "Hvor meget vejer det?" (How much does it weigh?)

hvor som helst.explanation: "Hvor som helst" means "anywhere". The ending "som helst" also follows other question words: "hvem som helst" (anyone), "hvad som helst" (anything) and "hvornår som helst" (any time).

hvordan.explanation: "Hvordan" means "how". To ask how old someone is, use "hvor" (how) before the word instead: "Hvor gammel er du?" (How old are you?) To ask how many, do the same: "Hvor mange børn har du?" (How many children do you have?)

hvordan går det?.explanation: "Hvordan går det?" means "How's it going?". Literally, it is "how goes it". To ask the other person back after you answer, add "og dig?" (and you?): "Det går godt, og dig?" (It's going well, and you?)

hvordan har du det?.explanation: "Hvordan har du det?" means "How are you?". Literally, it is "how have you it". To answer, say "Jeg har det godt" (I'm doing well) or "Fint, tak" (Fine, thanks).

hvorefter.explanation: "Hvorefter" means "after which". It is built from "hvor" (which) and "efter" (after). To join two events in a simpler way, use "og så" (and then): "Hun lukkede bogen, og så slukkede hun lyset" (She closed the book, and then she turned off the light).

hvorfor.explanation: "Hvorfor" means "why". To give a reason, start your answer with "fordi" (because): "Hvorfor kommer du ikke?" "Fordi jeg er syg." (Why aren't you coming? Because I am sick.)

hvorfra.explanation: "Hvorfra" means "from where". It is built from "hvor" (where) and "fra" (from). The word "fra" (from) also ends the question "Hvor kommer du fra?" (Where do you come from?)

hvorimod.explanation: "Hvorimod" means "whereas". To contrast two statements, put it after a comma before the second one: "Jeg drikker kaffe, hvorimod hun drikker te" (I drink coffee, whereas she drinks tea). To say two things happen at the same time, use "mens" (while) instead: "Jeg læser, mens du sover" (I read while you sleep).

hvornår.explanation: "Hvornår" means "when" in a question. To say "when" in the middle of a sentence about the future, use "når" (when): "Jeg ringer, når jeg kommer hjem" (I will call when I get home). To say "when" about one finished event in the past, use "da" (when): "Jeg var glad, da du kom" (I was happy when you came).

hvorved.explanation: "Hvorved" means "whereby". It is built from "hvor" (where) and "ved" (by). To introduce the result of an action, put it after a comma that follows the action: "Han trykkede på knappen, hvorved døren gik op" (He pressed the button, whereby the door opened).

hvorvidt.explanation: "Hvorvidt" means "whether". It sounds formal. In everyday speech, use "om" (whether): "Jeg ved ikke, om han kommer" (I do not know whether he is coming).

hygge.explanation: "Hygge" means "cozy". It is a Danish idea of a warm, relaxed time with other people, candles and food. To say you are having a cozy time, use "at hygge sig" (to have a cozy time): "Vi hygger os" (We are having a cozy time).

hyggelig.explanation: "Hyggelig" means "cozy". It comes from "hygge" (a cozy time). To say a person is nice to be around, use it too: "Han er hyggelig" (He is nice to be around).

hyggeligt at møde dig.explanation: "Hyggeligt at møde dig" means "nice to meet you". Literally, it is "cozy to meet you". To reply, say "i lige måde" (likewise).

hyppig.explanation: "Hyppig" means "frequent". To describe how someone does something, use "hyppigt" (frequently): "Han besøger os hyppigt" (He visits us frequently).

hysterisk.explanation: "Hysterisk" means "hysterical". To say something is extremely funny, put it before "sjov" (funny): "hysterisk sjov" (hilariously funny).

hytteost.explanation: "Hytteost" means "cottage cheese". It is built from "hytte" (cottage) and "ost" (cheese). The word "ost" also ends "smøreost" (cheese you spread on bread).

håb.explanation: "Håb" means "a hope". To say you hope for something, use the verb "at håbe" (to hope): "Jeg håber, det virker" (I hope it works).

håbefuld.explanation: "Håbefuld" means "hopeful". It is built from "håb" (hope) and the ending "-fuld" (full of). The same ending is in "smertefuld" (painful).

håbløs.explanation: "Håbløs" means "hopeless". The ending "-løs" means "without", as in "hjemløs" (homeless). To say you are very bad at something, use it too: "Jeg er håbløs til matematik" (I am hopeless at math).

håndbagage.explanation: "Håndbagage" means "carry-on luggage". It is built from "hånd" (hand) and "bagage" (luggage). For the bags you hand in at check-in, say "indchecket bagage" (checked luggage): "Jeg har to stykker indchecket bagage" (I have two pieces of checked luggage).

håndbold.explanation: "Håndbold" means "handball". It is built from "hånd" (hand) and "bold" (ball). To talk about the sport, leave out the article: "Jeg spiller håndbold" (I play handball). To talk about the ball, use "en håndbold" (a handball): "Jeg kaster en håndbold" (I throw a handball).

hår.explanation: "Hår" means "a hair". Without an article, it means the hair on a head: "Jeg vasker mit hår" (I wash my hair). It starts other words, such as "hårfarve" (hair color).

hård.explanation: "Hård" means "hard", as in firm and not soft. To say a job is tough, use it too: "et hårdt job" (a tough job). For "hard" meaning "difficult", use "svær" (difficult) instead: "en svær opgave" (a difficult task).

hårdhudet.explanation: "Hårdhudet" means "thick-skinned". It is built from "hård" (hard) and "hud" (skin), with the ending "-et".

hævet.explanation: "Hævet" means "swollen". It comes from the verb "at hæve" (to raise). To say dough has risen, use the same word: "hævet dej" (risen dough).

hævn.explanation: "Hævn" means "revenge". To say someone takes revenge, use "at tage hævn" (to take revenge): "Han tog hævn" (He took revenge). The verb is "at hævne" (to avenge): "Hun vil hævne sin bror" (She wants to avenge her brother).

hø.explanation: "Hø" means "hay". Do not mix it up with "halm" (straw): "Hesten sover på halm" (The horse sleeps on straw).

høfeber.explanation: "Høfeber" means "hay fever". It is built from "hø" (hay) and "feber" (fever). The word "feber" also stands alone: "Jeg har feber" (I have a fever).

høflig.explanation: "Høflig" means "polite". To say how someone speaks, use "høfligt" (politely): "Hun taler høfligt" (She speaks politely).

høflighed.explanation: "Høflighed" means "politeness". It is built from "høflig" (polite) and the ending "-hed", which turns a describing word into a noun: "fri" (free) becomes "frihed" (freedom).

høj.explanation: "Høj" means "tall". To say how loud someone speaks, use "højt" (loudly): "Tal højt" (Speak loudly).

højlydt.explanation: "Højlydt" means "loud". It is built from "høj" (high) and "lyd" (sound). To say how someone does something, use it after the verb: "Hun lo højlydt" (She laughed loudly).

højre.explanation: "Højre" means "right", the opposite of left. To say turn right, use "til højre" (to the right): "Drej til højre" (Turn right).

højst.explanation: "Højst" means "at most". To say "highly" before a describing word, use it too: "højst interessant" (highly interesting).

højtidelig.explanation: "Højtidelig" means "solemn". To say how someone speaks, use "højtideligt" (solemnly): "Hun talte højtideligt" (She spoke solemnly).

hørelse.explanation: "Hørelse" means "hearing", as in the ability to hear. To say you listen to something on purpose, use "at lytte" (to listen): "Jeg lytter til musik" (I listen to music).

høretelefoner.explanation: "Høretelefoner" means "headphones". It is built from "at høre" (to hear) and "telefon" (phone). To say one set, use "et par" (a pair): "Jeg har købt et par høretelefoner" (I have bought a pair of headphones).

I.explanation: "I" means "you" when you speak to two or more people. For one person, use "du" (you): "Du er min ven" (You are my friend). To say "I" about yourself, use "jeg" (I): "Jeg bor i Aarhus" (I live in Aarhus). The small word "i" (in) is different: in "I bor i Aarhus" (You all live in Aarhus), the first "I" is "you (all)" and the second "i" is "in".

at iagttage.explanation: "At iagttage" means "to observe". To say you watch something on purpose to learn about it, use it: "Vi iagttager fuglene" (We observe the birds). To say you see something without trying, use "at se" (to see): "Jeg ser en fugl" (I see a bird).

at identificere.explanation: "At identificere" means "to identify". To say you prove who you are, add "sig" (yourself): "Jeg skal identificere mig" (I have to identify myself).

at igangsætte.explanation: "At igangsætte" means "to initiate". It sounds formal. To say an official body starts a study, say: "Ministeriet igangsætter en undersøgelse" (The ministry is starting a study). For a plain start, use "at starte" (to start): "Vi starter i morgen" (We start tomorrow).

at ignorere.explanation: "At ignorere" means "to ignore". To say someone pays no attention to messages, say: "Han ignorerer alle beskeder" (He ignores all messages). To say you overlook something by mistake, use "at overse" (to overlook): "Jeg overså skiltet" (I overlooked the sign).

at illustrere.explanation: "At illustrere" means "to illustrate", as in adding pictures to a book. It also means making something clear with an example: "Det illustrerer problemet" (That makes the problem clear).

at implementere.explanation: "At implementere" means "to implement". To say a company puts a new system into use, say: "Firmaet implementerer det nye system i dag" (The company is implementing the new system today).

at imponere.explanation: "At imponere" means "to impress". To say a speech impressed people, say: "Hendes tale imponerede os" (Her speech impressed us). To say you are impressed, use "imponeret" (impressed): "Jeg er imponeret" (I am impressed).

at importere.explanation: "At importere" means "to import". To say you bring files into a program, say: "Jeg importerer filer til programmet" (I import files into the program). The opposite is "at eksportere" (to export): "Danmark eksporterer bacon" (Denmark exports bacon).

at indbyde.explanation: "At indbyde" means "to invite". It sounds more formal than "at invitere" (to invite). To invite someone in an announcement, say: "Vi indbyder til generalforsamling" (We invite you to the general meeting). To invite a friend, use "at invitere": "Jeg inviterer dig til fest" (I invite you to a party).

at inddrage.explanation: "At inddrage" means "to involve". To say you bring someone into a decision, say: "Vi vil inddrage børnene i beslutningen" (We want to involve the children in the decision). It also means to take something away officially: "inddrage et kørekort" (to revoke a driver's license).

at indebære.explanation: "At indebære" means "to involve", as in having something as a necessary part. To say a change brings costs, say: "Ændringen indebærer flere udgifter" (The change involves more costs). To bring a person into something, use "at inddrage" (to involve) instead: "Vi inddrager børnene" (We involve the children).

at indeholde.explanation: "At indeholde" means "to contain". It is built from "inde" (inside) and "at holde" (to hold). To say a food has nuts in it, say: "Produktet indeholder nødder" (The product contains nuts).
